sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Vulcānus** (*vulcanus*) — The Smith of the Gods — belongs to the Roman tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "Fire, Forge, Craft". The name means "Possibly from fulgere (to flash) or a pre-Roman fire root"[^1].

Vulcānus is Rome's ambivalent fire: the destructive flame that must be kept outside the walls and the tamed forge-fire that arms the state. His festival burns fish alive in midsummer — not for food, but to buy the city's safety from the god who burns cities.[^2]

PuniCodex restores the name as **Vulcānus** and serves its temple at [vulcānus.com](https://xn--vulcnus-v3a.com). The original preserves one prosodic feature — stress or vowel length — rather than both, which places the name in Tier 2. The plain ASCII form *vulcanus* survives as a modern convenience imposed by the early domain-name system; the restoration, not the fallback, is the form the project defends as philologically complete[^3].

sources.citation: Lewis & Short, A Latin Dictionary, Oxford, Clarendon Press; Perseus digitization, 1879.
Ovid (Publius Ovidius Naso), Metamorphoses / Fasti / Heroides, Loeb Classical Library, 17.
Varro, De Lingua Latina / Antiquitates Rerum Divinarum, Loeb Classical Library, 45 BCE.

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, ASCII constraint, Unicode restoration, name variations, tier classification.
sections.body:
No indigenous written attestation survives for this name; **Vulcānus** is a scholarly transliteration of the reconstructed spoken form. Etymologically the name means "Possibly from fulgere (to flash) or a pre-Roman fire root"[^1].

The ASCII form *vulcanus* survives only because the early domain-name system could not carry diacritics; it is a technological compromise, not an ancient spelling. The Unicode restoration **Vulcānus** recovers the vowel length of the original directly in the address bar. The original preserves one prosodic feature — stress or vowel length — rather than both, which places the name in Tier 2.

The letter-by-letter transformation runs:

- **v** → **V** — Same letter
- **u** → **u** — Same letter
- **l** → **l** — Same letter
- **c** → **c** — Same letter
- **a** → **ā** — Macron marks the long vowel
- **n** → **n** — Same letter
- **u** → **u** — Same letter
- **s** → **s** — Same letter

The project holds the domain **vulcānus.com** (xn--vulcnus-v3a.com) as the canonical home of this name[^2].

sources.citation: Virgil (Publius Vergilius Maro), Aeneid / Eclogues / Georgics, Loeb Classical Library / Oxford Classical Texts, 19 BCE.
Ovid (Publius Ovidius Naso), Metamorphoses / Fasti / Heroides, Loeb Classical Library, 17.

sections.label: Pronunciation
sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/vulˈkaː.nus/** — Classical Latin.[^1]

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: vul-KAH-nus, long ā on the stressed second syllable.

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Latin** — Vulcānus
- **Greek twin** — Ἥφαιστος
- **Modern word** — volcano
- **Owned form** — Vulcānus

Latin Vulcānus — also Volcānus in inscriptions — scans with a long ā; its origin is pre-Roman and possibly Cretan (Wchanos has been proposed), making him one of the oldest names in the Roman pantheon. The macron marks the quantity on which the classical poets agree.

sources.citation: Lewis & Short, A Latin Dictionary, Oxford, Clarendon Press; Perseus digitization, 1879.

sections.body:
The original script for this roman name has not yet been added to PUNICODEX. The form shown is a scholarly transliteration.[^1]

The form **Vulcānus** is therefore a scholarly transliteration rather than an attested ancient spelling; it encodes the reconstructed sound of the name for modern use, and no mark in it is decorative.

sections.label: Domains & Attributes
sections.purpose: Sphere of influence, titles, epithets, domain cards.
sections.body:
Vulcānus is Rome's ambivalent fire: the destructive flame that must be kept outside the walls and the tamed forge-fire that arms the state. His festival burns fish alive in midsummer — not for food, but to buy the city's safety from the god who burns cities.[^1]

### Mulciber

"The Softener" — his title as the smith who coaxes iron, taming fire into craft.

### Volcanalia

August 23: live fish thrown into bonfires, a substitute-offering against the fire's hunger for the city.

### The Volcanal

His open-air altar in the Forum — above the Lapis Niger, at the city's oldest sacred ground.

### The Aeolian Forges

The island Vulcano, where his hammerings were heard beneath the smoking mountain.

sources.citation: Ovid (Publius Ovidius Naso), Metamorphoses / Fasti / Heroides, Loeb Classical Library, 17.

sections.label: Symbols
sections.body:
The iconography associated with Vulcānus concentrates in a small set of recurring attributes, each a compressed statement about the name:[^1]

- **The hammer** — Force made precise — the smith's answer to the flame
- **The tongs** — The hand's extension into fire; technology as safe distance
- **The bonfire** — Fire acknowledged and bargained with

sources.citation: Lewis & Short, A Latin Dictionary, Oxford, Clarendon Press; Perseus digitization, 1879.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
Roman myth borrowed Hēphaistos' stories for him, but his cult is older and darker than the smith of Olympos: Vulcānus is first the fire that must be averted.[^1]

### The Fish Fires (The Substitute)

At the Volcanalia, the hottest and driest month, Romans threw live fish from the Tiber into bonfires at the Volcanal. The calendars explain the rite as substitution: souls of water given to fire, so that fire takes the offering instead of the granaries. It is propitiation, not celebration — Rome's insurance premium paid in flame.[^2]

### Venus and Mars (The Net)

Ovid retells the Odyssey's finest comedy: Vulcānus, tipped off by the Sun, forges a net finer than a spider's thread and catches his wife Venus in bed with Mars. The gods gather to laugh — and the myth carries its Roman moral: craft exposes what force cannot guard. The cuckolded smith is also the only god who ever shamed war itself.

### The Binding Chair (The Throne)

The Roman version of the Hēphaistos cycle kept the revenge on Iūnō: Vulcānus sent his mother a golden throne that bound her fast when she sat — payment for being thrown from heaven at birth — and only wine, brought by Bacchus, persuaded the limping god to come loose her. Even the queen of heaven learns that the forge holds the stronger magic.

### Aeneas' Shield (The Arming)

The Aeneid gives him his noblest commission: at Venus' plea, Vulcānus forges the arms of Aeneas, and on the shield he works the future of Rome — Actium, the triumphs, the unborn empire — "the fame and fate of his descendants." The smith-god is thus the secret author of Roman destiny: history itself as forge-work.

sources.citation: Ovid (Publius Ovidius Naso), Metamorphoses / Fasti / Heroides, Loeb Classical Library, 17.
Varro, De Lingua Latina / Antiquitates Rerum Divinarum, Loeb Classical Library, 45 BCE.

sections.label: Syncretism & Reception
sections.purpose: Cross-cultural identification, later adaptations, and interpretatio.
sections.body:
His equation with Hēphaistos is complete in art, but Rome insisted on the difference: Vulcānus is fire as danger, kept at arm's length — his oldest shrine outside the pomerium, his temple on the Campus Martius. Through Vulcano island his name fused with every smoking mountain; through the Aeolian forges he merged with the Cyclopes. The word "volcano" is his inheritance, which no other god can claim: a deity's name become a category of the planet.[^1]

Within the Roman tradition, closely related names in the corpus include [[diana|Diāna]], [[ianus|Iānus]], [[iuno|Iūnō]], [[iuppiter|Iūppiter]], [[neptunus|Neptūnus]], and [[hephaistos|Hēphaistos]].

sources.citation: Lewis & Short, A Latin Dictionary, Oxford, Clarendon Press; Perseus digitization, 1879.

sections.label: Cultural Legacy
sections.purpose: Modern influence, literature, art, popular culture, and contemporary practice.
sections.body: Vulcanization — Goodyear's process for rubber — borrowed his name for fire's mastery of matter; volcanoes, volcanology, and a Star Trek homeworld followed. In Rome he gave his title Mulciber to every poet's image of gentle strength. The deeper legacy is conceptual: he embodies technology's eternal contract — the same fire that forges the shield burns the city — and every safety code is his Volcanalia continued by other means.[^1]

sources.citation: Lewis & Short, A Latin Dictionary, Oxford, Clarendon Press; Perseus digitization, 1879.

sections.label: Archaeology & Material Evidence
sections.purpose: Sites, inscriptions, artifacts, and physical attestations.
sections.body: The Volcanal in the Forum — an open precinct above the Lapis Niger, with the archaic dedication of a Senate's honorific to the god — anchors his cult in Rome's oldest ground. Vulcano in the Aeolian islands preserves the fumarole fields the ancients called his workshops, and the islands' obsidian industry fed Neolithic trade millennia before the myths. Pompeii's forges, with their anvils and half-finished work, show his everyday cult of the artisans who kept his festival as their own holiday.[^1]

sources.citation: Lewis & Short, A Latin Dictionary, Oxford, Clarendon Press; Perseus digitization, 1879.

sections.label: Epithets & Epicleses
sections.body:
His titles divide, as he does, between the dangerous fire and the tamed.

- **Mulciber** — 'the Softener'; the smith's title, fire as craft, used by all the poets.
- **Quietus** — 'the Stilled'; the averted fire, worshipped so it stays asleep.
- **Armipotens** — 'powerful in arms'; the forger of the state's weapons.
- **Ignipotens** — 'lord of fire'; the full epic style.
- **Volcanus** — the older spelling of his name, kept in the oldest inscriptions and the island that immortalized it.

sources.citation: Virgil, Aeneid 8; the Volcanal inscriptions.

sections.label: Oracle & Cult Sites
sections.body: The **Volcanal** in the Roman Forum — the open-air precinct above the Lapis Niger, beside the archaic inscription of Rome's oldest law — was his oldest seat, deliberately outside the city's sacred boundary: the dangerous fire worshipped at arm's length. His temple stood on the Campus Martius, likewise outside the walls. The **Aeolian island of Vulcano**, with its smoking fumaroles, was shown to travelers as his forge-chimney; its ancient obsidian industry — worked since the Neolithic — made the myth practical geology long before it was theology.

sources.citation: Dionysius 2.50 (the Volcanal); Thucydides 3.88 (the islands).

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body:
Vulcānus is the god of the firewall. He teaches that the power worth having is the power kept at the right distance: fire in the forge, not the bedroom; strength in the net, not the fist. Every craftsperson who has burned a hand learning the distance knows his liturgy — and every city that survives the summer pays his quiet premium.

His contract is written now in building codes and reactor protocols, in firewalls and safety factors: the fire is not the enemy — the distance is the discipline. Rome worshipped him outside the walls on purpose, and every civilization since has redrawn that line where the useful flame ends and the other kind begins. To keep a forge is to renegotiate his treaty daily, in steel, in silica, in code.[^1]

sources.citation: Lewis & Short, A Latin Dictionary, Oxford, Clarendon Press; Perseus digitization, 1879.
